column2: Indirect water consumption from electricity generation substantially exceeds direct on-site cooling water consumption across empirical and macro-models: direct cooling water is 1.30e8 m3 in P02 (pdf p. 8, EXT-033) and 140 billion L in P04 (pdf p. 5, EXT-070); off-site electricity-embedded water is 3.83e8 m3 in P02 (pdf p. 8, EXT-034) and 1,225 billion L in P04 (pdf p. 9, EXT-076). The resulting ratios are derived [I], calculated from EXT-033 and EXT-034 for P02 as: (3.83e8 m3 / 1.30e8 m3 = 2.95x), and derived [I], calculated from EXT-070 and EXT-076 for P04 as: (1,225B L / 140B L = 8.75x [roughly 9x]). In the IEA baseline cited by P04, the ratio is derived [I], calculated from EXT-070 and EXT-075 as: (373B L / 140B L = 2.66x, pdf p. 7). (Note: P02 and P04 report the underlying volumes; the multiplier ratios are derived [I] and not printed findings of the papers).

column2:
Data centre exposure to water stress varies significantly by geographical scale and hydrological metric, comprising four distinct empirical findings (thresholds reported only where printed in the paper):
(1) AWARE share of direct water: ~20% of direct data centre water footprint comes from watersheds experiencing moderate to high water stress (P02, Siddik et al., pdf p. 3, EXT-022; EXT-023; Year: 2018 fleet model; Geography: United States subbasins, EXT-028; Metric: ISO 14046 AWARE characterization factor, EXT-030; numerical CF threshold not stated in the paper).
(2) Share of facilities in stressed areas by study:
  - Global facilities: 25% of data centers experience at least 1 month of water gap annually under baseline hydrologic conditions (P05, Rosa et al., pdf p. 1, EXT-082; evaluated across all 9,347 data centers identified globally, EXT-081; Publication date: DATE NOT PRINTED; Data year: 2025, pdf p. 1; Metric: process-based monthly water gaps where demand exceeds available renewable supply, EXT-093; numerical percentage threshold not stated in the paper). Under future hydrologic conditions, affected facilities rise to 33% (pdf p. 1, EXT-083).
  - US facilities: 32% of data centres are within areas of high or extremely high water stress (P09, Planet Tracker, pdf p. 3, EXT-147; evaluated across US data centres mapped across river basins, EXT-148; Publication date: DATE NOT PRINTED [file carries banner 'PLANET TRACKER · SEPTEMBER 2024'; not verified at original website]; Metric: WRI Aqueduct water stress categories, EXT-148; numerical percentage threshold not stated in the paper; NOTE: strictly US data centres, not global; no stable page; cite section and paragraph; pdf_page is locator in my file, not a page of the source).
(3) Asia-specific share: 41% of Asian data centres are located in areas of extremely high water stress, and a further 22% in the high category (P08, Planet Tracker, pdf p. 2, EXT-182; Publication date: DATE NOT PRINTED [file carries banner 'PLANET TRACKER · MARCH 2025'; not verified at original website]; Data year: DataCenterMap accessed 2 March 2025, pdf p. 2; Metric: WRI Aqueduct ratio of total water demand to available renewable supply, EXT-181; numerical percentage threshold not stated in the paper; P08 notes 'risk thresholds fall into 5 categories from low to extremely high', pdf p. 2, EXT-181; no stable page; cite section and paragraph; pdf_page is locator in my file, not a page of the source).
(4) Share of hubs in stressed metros: 52% of global data centre hubs are located in high water-stress regions, rising to 58% by 2050 (P10, Baringa, pdf p. 3, EXT-158; Publication date: November 2025, pdf p. 1; Geography: Global data centre market hubs; Metric: Baringa Market Attractiveness Index with Aqueduct WRI overlays; numerical percentage threshold not stated in the paper).

column19: Data centre capacity in India is concentrated in four metropolitan markets: Mumbai leads, followed by Chennai, Hyderabad, and Bengaluru, where competing urban water demands are already high (P07, pdf pp. 2, 15, EXT-189, EXT-207). Future empirical research question for dissertation dataset: Does this metropolitan clustering intersect with localized groundwater overdraft in surrounding districts?

column2: Data centre siting decisions prioritize electrical grid capacity, fiber latency, and land availability over hydrological sustainability, creating regional clusters in vulnerable watersheds.
column4: YES

column18: EXT-102 (pdf p. 8, P05) and EXT-212 (pdf p. 19, P07) cite emerging policy frameworks (e.g. Andhra Pradesh offering specific subsidies for coastal seawater-cooled data centres, and municipal zoning requiring recycled water), indicating that emerging regulations are beginning to force water considerations into late-stage siting approvals.
column19: Do Indian state data centre policies consider water constraints? P07 documents that state policies heavily focus on power tariff subsidies and infrastructure incentives while water efficiency and cooling standards are largely absent or emerging (P07, pdf pp. 18–19, EXT-209, EXT-213). Siting continues to prioritize electrical grid capacity and fiber landing infrastructure (17 international subsea cables at 14 landing stations, EXT-198) rather than water availability (P07, pdf pp. 2, 10, EXT-188, EXT-198).

column2: Critical transparency and disclosure deficit: public, verified facility-level water consumption telemetry is absent for the vast majority of commercial and colocation data centres (P01 notes less than a third of operators measure water consumption, pdf p. 1, EXT-003; P02 notes absence of public commercial facility data, pdf p. 11, EXT-038; P04 notes omission of per-facility water metrics, pdf p. 7, 8, EXT-074, EXT-078; P06 notes wide reporting deficit across 31 studies, pdf p. 3, 48, EXT-109, EXT-125; P07 documents confidentiality of operator water data in India, pdf p. 14, 16, EXT-205, EXT-207).

column18: EXT-069 (pdf p. 5, P04) and EXT-048 (pdf p. 2, P03) note that hyperscale market leaders (Meta and Microsoft) disclose annual corporate-wide water consumption broken down by source (potable, non-potable, recycled) and publish global average WUE benchmarks, demonstrating partial voluntary reporting among top-tier operators.
column19: Do Indian regulatory authorities possess empirical facility-level water telemetry? P07 documents that facility water consumption is treated as commercially confidential by Indian operators and is not publicly tracked (P07, pdf p. 14, 16, EXT-205, EXT-207).

column2: Thermodynamic water-energy trade-off: transitioning from evaporative cooling to dry air cooling eliminates on-site water consumption but incurs an operational electricity penalty (increased facility power consumption to drive airflow fans and cooling compressors), shifting environmental burdens to off-site power generation and indirect grid water consumption (P02, pdf p. 10, EXT-040; P06, pdf pp. 4, 18, EXT-110, EXT-116; P10, pdf pp. 4, 5, 8, EXT-164, EXT-165, EXT-171). (Note: The specific 20% to 40% numerical penalty is a single-source finding from P10 only, reported in SSF-06).
column4: YES
column16: P02 (ERL subbasin trade-offs), P06 (Masanet engineering equations), and P10 (Baringa empirical operational data) independently demonstrate this thermodynamic penalty across distinct modeling approaches.
column17: No merging required: P02 (environmental trade-off modeling across 2,118 subbasins), P06 (thermodynamic engineering review equations), and P10 (empirical commercial data on European data centre retrofits) evaluate this trade-off independently without shared empirical datasets. Confirmed independent lineages = 3 (>=2).
column18: EXT-140 (pdf p. 3, P09) and EXT-019 (pdf p. 4, P01) highlight that advanced two-phase immersion cooling and underwater data centres eliminate evaporative water consumption without cooling fan energy penalties, achieving high thermal efficiency without water loss.
column19: Would mandating dry cooling in India's hot climate increase electricity consumption and off-site power grid water use? Not modeled in P01–P14. The literature establishes the qualitative thermodynamic trade-off (P02, EXT-040; P06, EXT-110; P10, EXT-164), but the resulting grid water trade-off across India's regional power grids remains an unaddressed empirical question.

column2:
Hyperscale facilities achieve significantly superior nominal water and power efficiency compared to enterprise facilities, but their massive absolute capacity creates severe localized hydrological point-source pressure. The literature reports two separate modeling benchmarks for a 100-MW facility (not a single range):
  (1) Daily benchmark: ~2 million litres of water per day for a typical 100-MW hyperscale facility (cited from IEA by P07, CEEW, pdf pp. 8, 13, EXT-197, EXT-201). In annual terms, this equates to derived [I], calculated from EXT-197 as: (2,000,000 L/day * 365 days) / 10^9 = 0.73 billion L/year.
  (2) Annual benchmark: 2.5 billion litres of water each year for a single 100-MW hyperscale facility using evaporative cooling—enough to supply more than 80,000 people (P10, Baringa, pdf p. 3, EXT-156; pdf p. 8, EXT-160).
These figures contrast with a medium 15-MW facility using water equivalent to 3 average hospitals or two 18-hole golf courses (P01, Mytton, pdf p. 1, EXT-007; Masanet, P06, pdf pp. 5, 12, EXT-111, EXT-114).
column16: P01, P06, and P10 independently evaluate hyperscale vs enterprise efficiency metrics and localized water withdrawal impacts.
column17: No merging required: P01 (synthesis of US hyperscale PUEs vs enterprise), P06 (academic literature meta-analysis of data center scales), and P10 (consultancy engineering modeling of 100-MW facilities) represent 3 distinct independent lineages. Confirmed independent lineages = 3 (>=2).
column18: EXT-161 (pdf p. 3, P10) notes that over 40% of newly announced hyperscale capacity since 2023 is shifting toward low- or no-water cooling designs, meaning future hyperscale campuses will not all rely on traditional evaporative cooling towers.
column19: A 100-MW hyperscale facility consumes ~2 million litres of water per day (cited from IEA by P07, pdf p. 8, EXT-197; derived [I]: 0.73 billion L/year) or 2.5 billion litres annually under evaporative cooling (enough to supply more than 80,000 people, P10, pdf p. 3, EXT-156). In Indian metropolitan clusters, this creates localized point-source competition with municipal supplies and private tankers (P07, pdf pp. 8, 15, EXT-197, EXT-207).
